Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

KABUL, Afghanistan (CNN)  -- Babies lie side by side in warming beds or sprawled on blankets atop crude wooden tables. Many families at Indira Gandhi Children's Hospital in Kabul, Afghanistan, seem resigned to the situation. Children with wounds and broken bones are carried in by their parents to wait on stiff plastic chairs. Outside, coughing youngsters squat on the pavement with their anxious families, waiting for care. And everywhere, parents clutch plastic bags containing bring-your-own medicines and supplies. For though they are all awaiting treatment at Afghanistan's only specialist pediatric hospital, the hospital cannot even afford bandages for its patients. The Indira Gandhi Children's Hospital in central Kabul has to run on an operating budget of less than $1,200 a month, said Dr. Noorulhaq Yousufzai, the hospital director. The few supplies that he can buy have to be hoarded for emergencies, and he has to count on parents to buy what's needed to care for their children. "In some cases, there is shortage of the surgical materials, and sometimes we don't have antiseptic to use," Yousufzai said. The United Nations says that more than $15 billion in aid has been sent to Afghanistan since the U.S.-led coalition overthrew the Taliban in late 2001. But still, the hospital cannot afford to help the hundreds of children who stream in every day, desperate for care and cures. The government does pay for salaries and sometimes for fuel, but there is often a shortage of even basic supplies like syringes. Doctors say they have to double up premature babies in incubators. And some of those incubators are compromised. On a recent day, a plastic surgical mask taped onto one machine was the only shield from infection.  Watch scenes from inside the hospital » . The parents waiting anxiously beside their sick children seem resigned to the situation in the hospital. One mother, who declined to give her name, said she spent the family's entire weekly income of $8 on an injection that did not help her baby. "This is something that the hospital should be giving us, because we can't afford it," she said. The U.S. Agency for International Development says infant mortality has dropped by 22 percent since the overthrow of the Taliban but acknowledges that the health status for Afghans is among the worst in the world. One in every five Afghan children will die before their 5th birthday, often of a preventable disease, according to the Save the Children aid agency. The toll on the children and parents is clear to any visitor, and the strain hits the hospital staff, too. "When you see a patient is very, very, sick and you cannot help, and they have to provide something for their children and they are not able to provide, it's also a stress for us," Yousufzai said. At the end of 2001, there were hopes that the hospital would be upgraded, but it is still waiting. It needs some acute care of its own, or it will continue to struggle to help the children who arrive at its door pleading for care.

**Title:** Inside Kabul’s Only Pediatric Hospital: Where International Aid Fails and Babies Share Incubators

**KABUL, Afghanistan —** In the dimly lit wards of the Indira Gandhi Children's Hospital, the sound of wheezing infants and the rhythmic beep of monitors are punctuated by a quiet, pervasive desperation. As Kabul’s sole specialized pediatric facility, the hospital is supposed to be a sanctuary for the nation’s sickest children. Instead, it has become a grim symbol of a broken system, operating on a meager budget of less than $1,200 a month—a crippling pittance for a facility tasked with saving thousands of lives.

Despite the tens of billions of dollars in international aid that have poured into Afghanistan over the last two decades, virtually none of that wealth appears to have trickled down to the hospital's bare shelves. The facility suffers from a catastrophic shortage of the most basic medical necessities, from life-saving antibiotics and IV fluids to simple bandages and sterile syringes. 

To keep the hospital from collapsing entirely, the burden of funding basic care has been shifted onto those least able to afford it: the patients’ families. 

In the hospital’s courtyard, destitute parents—many of whom have traveled for days from remote, war-torn provinces—are routinely handed handwritten lists by doctors. They are instructed to go to local private pharmacies to purchase the gloves, needles, and medicines required to treat their own dying children. For families surviving on less than a dollar a day, a single prescription can represent a month’s income. Those who cannot raise the funds are forced to watch helplessly as their children’s conditions deteriorate without intervention.

Inside the intensive care and neonatal units, the resource drought forces medical staff to make agonizing compromises daily. Overwhelmed by the sheer volume of critically ill infants and crippled by a shortage of functional equipment, doctors are regularly forced to double up, or even triple up, premature newborns in single, compromised incubators. Many of these aging machines lack reliable temperature controls or steady power supplies, heightening the risk of infection and cross-contamination between vulnerable babies. 

"We are practicing medicine in the dark," said one senior pediatrician, speaking on condition of anonymity. "We know how to save these babies, but our hands are tied. When you have two premature infants in one failing incubator, and you are reusing single-use tubes because you have no choice, you are not providing modern medicine—you are engaged in a daily battle against impossible odds."

The dire reality at Indira Gandhi Children’s Hospital exposes a monumental disconnect between global aid pledges and on-the-ground reality. Years of bureaucratic mismanagement, systemic corruption, misallocated foreign assistance, and recent political isolation have severed the connection between international humanitarian funds and Afghanistan's crucial public health infrastructure. 

While aid agencies and international donors debate policy and conditionality in distant capitals, the real-world consequence of their systemic failure is borne by Afghanistan's youngest and most vulnerable citizens. Without immediate, direct intervention and a structural overhaul of how aid is delivered to primary healthcare facilities, Kabul’s premier children’s hospital will remain not a beacon of hope, but a stark reminder of a humanitarian promise left unfulfilled.

As the political and cultural heart of the nation, events in Kabul have consistently reshaped the geopolitical landscape of Central Asia and the wider world. 

The global public's perception of these events has largely been shaped through the lens of international journalism. A pivotal moment in this relationship occurred in August 2021 during the withdrawal of Western forces and the rapid return of the Taliban to power. As chaos engulfed the capital, **CNN** became one of the primary windows through which millions across the globe witnessed history unfolding in real time.

During those tense days, CNN correspondents—most notably Chief International Correspondent Clarissa Ward—remained on the ground in Kabul, delivering fearless, live reports amidst extraordinary danger. Broadcasting from the chaotic streets and outside the gates of Hamid Karzai International Airport, CNN captured the harrowing reality of desperate citizens attempting to flee, the sudden curtailment of freedoms, and the profound uncertainty facing the nation. Their coverage brought an unfiltered, human face to a complex political crisis, highlighting the fears of Afghan women and the immense risks taken by local journalists and fixers.

Today, reporting from Afghanistan presents unprecedented challenges. Media freedom in Kabul has been heavily restricted, and many local outlets have been forced to close. Yet, the ongoing coverage by networks like CNN remains vital. Through periodic on-the-ground reports and continuous analysis, international news organizations continue to shine a light on Afghanistan’s severe economic hardships, the ban on girls' education, and the ongoing humanitarian crises.

The stories coming out of Kabul serve as a crucial reminder to the world. Through the dedicated reporting of networks like CNN, the international community is forced to stay engaged with Afghanistan, ensuring that the voices and struggles of its people are not forgotten in the shadows of global news cycles.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article reporting on the severe shortage of medical supplies and dire financial situation at Indira Gandhi Children's Hospital in Kabul, Afghanistan. Include quotes from the hospital director, Dr. Noorulhaq Yousufzai.
counterfactuals.output:
**KABUL, Afghanistan (CNN) —** In the dimly lit, overcrowded wards of Kabul’s Indira Gandhi Children’s Hospital, the fragile cries of sick infants echo down cold, concrete corridors. Here, in Afghanistan's premier pediatric facility, doctors are fighting an increasingly unwinnable battle against disease, starvation, and a catastrophic lack of basic medical supplies.

Three years after the Taliban’s return to power precipitated a freeze on international aid and foreign bank assets, the healthcare infrastructure in the country is crumbling. Nowhere is the human toll of this economic freeze more visible than at Indira Gandhi Children’s Hospital, where infants share rusted beds and life-saving drugs have become a rare luxury.

"We are running on empty," said Dr. Noorulhaq Yousufzai, the director of the hospital, his voice heavy with exhaustion. "If international aid organizations and donors do not step in immediately, we will be forced to turn away thousands of sick children every month. We are watching preventable deaths happen right in front of our eyes."

### 'Parents expect a miracle'

The 360-bed hospital is currently operating well above capacity, housing as many as two or three malnourished babies to a single crib. Doctors report severe shortages of essential medicines, including pediatric antibiotics, painkillers, intravenous fluids, and specialized nutritional formulas required to treat acute malnutrition. 

Even basic consumables—gloves, clean syringes, and gauze—are rationed daily.

"Parents bring their dying babies to us expecting a miracle," Dr. Yousufzai told CNN from his office, surrounded by stacks of urgent requisition forms that the hospital simply lacks the funds to fulfill. "But sometimes we don't even have simple pain relief or clean needles to give them. It breaks our hearts every single day."

The financial situation at the facility is equally dire. Operating budgets have been slashed, leaving the hospital struggling to pay for basic utilities like fuel for winter heating and diesel for electricity generators needed to keep oxygen machines running. Many medical staff members have gone months without receiving their full salaries, yet they continue to report for duty.

### A compounding humanitarian crisis

The crisis at the hospital is a microcosm of Afghanistan's broader humanitarian disaster. According to the United Nations, over 23 million people in Afghanistan require humanitarian assistance, with women and children bearing the brunt of the hardship. Malnutrition rates have soared as poverty grips the country, driving record numbers of desperate families to the doors of Indira Gandhi Children's Hospital.

Many mothers walk for days from remote provinces, bringing critically ill children in the late stages of pneumonia, measles, or severe dehydration, only to find a facility struggling to keep its own lights on.

"We are treating the symptoms of a much larger economic collapse," Dr. Yousufzai said. "When families cannot afford food, the children fall ill. When they come to us, we don't have the resources to heal them. It is a vicious cycle."

### A plea to the international community

While international sanctions remain in place targeting the ruling Taliban regime, humanitarian organizations have repeatedly warned that blanket financial restrictions are paralyzing the public health sector. Though some emergency aid flows through non-governmental organizations, hospital administrators say it is a drop in the ocean compared to what is required to keep a national pediatric hospital operational.

Dr. Yousufzai issued a direct appeal to global leaders and international health organizations, urging them to decouple humanitarian medical relief from geopolitics.

"Politics should not cost a child their life," Dr. Yousufzai said. "The children lying in these beds know nothing of sanctions or governments. They only know pain and hunger. Humanity must come before political stances, before it is too late for an entire generation."

**BETWEEN HOPE AND HEARTBREAK: INSIDE KABUL’S OVERBURDENED PEDIATRIC HOSPITAL**

**KABUL, Afghanistan —** In the dimly lit corridors of the Indira Gandhi Holy Children’s Hospital, the dominant sound is a haunting chorus of weak, raspy crying. It is a sound that fills every corner of Afghanistan’s premier pediatric facility—a stark, physical echo of a nation’s ongoing humanitarian crisis.

In Ward 4, the malnutrition unit, two-year-old Omaid lies motionless on a metal framed bed. His skin, stretched thin over protruding ribs, resembles brittle parchment. Beside him sits his mother, Farzana, 26, continuously smoothing his brow with a frayed scarf. She traveled over twelve hours by shared taxi from the rugged hills of Wardak province to get here. 

"In our village, the clinic had no medicine, no doctors, nothing," Farzana whispers, her eyes hollowed by fatigue. "I sold my wedding ring to pay for the journey. If he dies here, I have nothing left to go home to."

Farzana’s story is not an exception; it is the daily reality for hundreds of families who flock to this Kabul landmark. Built decades ago and repeatedly battered by the country’s turbulent history, Indira Gandhi Hospital now stands as the last line of defense for Afghanistan’s most vulnerable population: its children.

### A System Scraped to the Bone

Since the political transition in August 2021 and the subsequent freezing of international development aid, Afghanistan’s public healthcare sector has been hovering on the brink of total collapse. While emergency humanitarian aid has prevented a complete blackout, major institutions like Indira Gandhi are functioning under unimaginable strain.

Dr. Ahmad, a senior pediatrician who asked that only his first name be used, walks the crowded wards with a clip board and a heavy heart. His face bears the quiet exhaustion of a man fighting a war with insufficient ammunition.

"We are designed to care for roughly 300 patients," Dr. Ahmad says, gesturing toward a room where three infants share a single hospital bed. "On any given day, we have 600, sometimes 700 children. We do not have enough beds, we do not have enough oxygen concentrators, and frequently, we run out of basic antibiotics."

The hospital staff face their own quiet battle. Many doctors and nurses have gone months without full salaries, living on reduced stipends provided by international aid agencies. Yet, they continue to report for duty.

"How can I stay home?" Dr. Ahmad asks, watching a nurse adjust an intravenous line on a struggling infant. "If we leave, these children die. So we stay. We buy medicine for poor patients out of our own pockets when we can. But our pockets are empty now, too."

### The Silent Epidemic

While pneumonia, measles, and preventable infections fill the wards, the underlying driver behind almost every admission is malnutrition. According to United Nations agencies, millions of Afghan children face acute food insecurity, driven by a lingering economic crisis, severe droughts, and widespread unemployment.

A severely malnourished child’s immune system is virtually non-existent. A common cold or mild bout of diarrhea—easily treatable in developed nations—becomes a swift death sentence in Kabul.

In the hospital’s Intensive Care Unit, the battle is at its most acute. Here, the hum of vital sign monitors is constantly interrupted by power fluctuations, forcing staff to rely on backup generators that consume precious fuel.

"Every night is a series of impossible choices," says one pediatric resident. "When you have two babies in critical respiratory distress and only one working ventilator, how do you choose? As a doctor, that is a choice you should never have to make. It stays with you forever."

### Fighting for a Future

Despite the pervasive gloom, there are moments of profound resilience. In the recovery ward, a young father cradles his eight-month-old daughter, who has finally begun to gain weight after three weeks of intensive therapeutic feeding. A faint smile breaks across his weathered face as she wraps her tiny fingers around his thumb.

It is these small victories that keep the hospital’s doors open. 

As night falls over Kabul, the winter air grows bitter cold. Outside the hospital gates, dozens of parents wrap themselves in heavy blankets, sleeping on the pavement, waiting for morning visiting hours, waiting for updates, waiting for a miracle.

Inside, Dr. Ahmad prepares for another long night shift. 

"The world may have moved on from Afghanistan, but the crisis has not moved on from us," he says, stepping back into the crowded ward. "These children are innocent. They did not create this politics, nor this economy. They just want to live."

counterfactuals.output:
**KABUL, Afghanistan** — Outside the rusted iron gates of the Indira Gandhi Children’s Hospital, Mohammad Isa holds a scrap of paper like a lifeline. On it, a doctor has scribbled a handwritten list of items required to treat his three-year-old daughter’s severe pneumonia: a pair of sterile latex gloves, a 10-cent plastic syringe, an intravenous catheter, and a small roll of medical tape.

"The doctors told me they have the medicine, but they don't even have a needle to give it to her," Isa says, his hands trembling as he counts out his remaining Afghanis. "I had to sell my wife’s ring to afford the bus ride from Ghazni. Now I am searching the street pharmacies just to buy the plastic tube that will keep my daughter alive."

This is the daily reality inside Kabul’s primary pediatric facility—a hospital that stands as a stark monument to the tragic disconnect between global humanitarian promises and on-the-ground reality.

Between 2001 and 2021, the international community poured unprecedented wealth into Afghanistan. The U.S. government alone spent more than $145 billion on reconstruction, according to reports from the Special Inspector General for Afghanistan Reconstruction (SIGAR), with billions more contributed by European allies, the World Bank, and non-governmental organizations. Millions of these dollars were explicitly earmarked to build a modern, resilient healthcare infrastructure. 

Yet inside the wards of Indira Gandhi Children's Hospital, that vast torrent of capital seems to have evaporated, leaving behind a barren institution where survival often depends on whether a destitute family can afford a few cents' worth of basic consumables.

### Wards of Desperation

Inside the hospital, the air is thick with the sound of crying infants and the heavy heat of overcrowded rooms. In many beds, two or three frail children are laid side-by-side, their mothers sitting at the foot of the mattress, fanning them with pieces of cardboard. 

The medical staff—highly trained and deeply dedicated—work under soul-crushing conditions. Many went months without pay following the Taliban’s return to power in August 2021 and the subsequent freeze on foreign aid assets. While emergency funding from agencies like the World Bank and the Red Cross has periodically stepped in to cover basic salaries, operational budgets remain severely eroded.

"It is a psychological torture for a doctor," says one senior pediatrician, speaking on the condition of anonymity due to political sensitivities. "We have the medical knowledge to save these children. But when a child enters shock, and we do not even have an IV line in the triage room, we must send a frantic father running into the street to buy one. Minutes matter. Sometimes, by the time they return with the supplies, it is too late."

The routine is systemic. The hospital’s central dispensary is often devoid of elementary items: gauze, rubbing alcohol, saline bags, and basic antibiotics. Parents can be seen crisscrossing the dusty street outside the hospital, where dozens of private pharmacies have capitalized on the hospital’s shortages, selling basic medical supplies at marked-up prices to desperate families.

### Where Did the Billions Go?

The abysmal state of pediatric care highlights the systemic failures that plagued the two-decade international intervention in Afghanistan. 

Audits by SIGAR and independent watchdogs have repeatedly detailed how billions of dollars in aid were lost to rampant corruption, inefficient foreign contracting, administrative overhead, and ill-conceived "ghost projects"—facilities built on paper or constructed poorly and left without sustainable funding. Millions were funneled through layers of international consultants before reaching local institutions, while systemic graft within the former Western-backed Afghan Ministry of Public Health siphoned off crucial resources.

When the U.S.-led coalition abruptly departed in 2021 and the Western-backed government collapsed, the fragile illusion of self-reliance crumbled. The immediate suspension of direct international aid—which had previously funded roughly 75 percent of the country’s public spending, including the vast national health network known as the *Sehatmandi* project—pulled the financial rug from beneath the healthcare system overnight.

International sanctions, bank transfers blockades, and the Taliban administration’s restrictions on women—who make up a vital portion of the healthcare workforce—have further compounded the crisis, crippling the delivery of humanitarian aid.

### The Human Toll

International aid agencies continue to warn that Afghanistan's healthcare system is on life support, sustained only by emergency humanitarian interventions that act as short-term band-aids rather than permanent solutions. 

Meanwhile, the human toll is measured in the quiet, daily tragedies unfolding in Kabul’s hospital corridors.

Back outside the pharmacy, Mohammad Isa hands over his last few coins for a roll of medical tape and a single catheter, wrapping them carefully in a plastic bag to bring back to his daughter’s bedside.

"They told us for twenty years that the world was rebuilding Afghanistan, that billions were coming to help us," Isa says, turning back toward the hospital entrance. "Where did it go? Because today, in the capital city, a child can die for want of a piece of plastic."
